Last year I had a large part of my yard cleared and turned into mulch. A lot of the trees here were eucalyptus and gum trees and the mulch pile was pretty big. Today I was cleaning up a side of my property covered in wild black berries and weeds. It is against a neighbors fence and I will be planting a small vineyard next to it.

To ensure that the black berries do not try to grow through the ground and to stop weeds growing so I do not need to tend to them later, I laid the newly cleared ground with newspaper and started to shovel mulch from last years pile. The edges of the pile had already started to decompose, so I started with them. After a bit I started to notice there were a lot of earth worms in the mix. I started to save a few by throwing them into a nearby garden. I thought it was a bit weird as this mulch was pretty acidic due to being mostly eucalyptus. I noticed a couple of really large australian earthworms pop up and they are dream for where I live. They are longer than my hand, very weather tolerant and they eat absolutely anything, but they breed very slowly. I breed them in a worm farm. So far I have only seen young worms once a year. I continue to dig away at the edge of the mulch and eventually hit the dry center and the worms disappear. I go to unload the mulch I have collected and noticed another large worm amongst the dry mulch. I almost missed it as it is the same colour. I grab him and put him into a nearby garden and then I stop for a moment and consider the situation. I go back to the mulch pile and start sifting through the top wet layer way above ground level and find that there are tonnes of large worms living in the top of the pile.

I decide to get a bucket and pick them out as a sift and shovel the mulch. It takes me 50-60% extra time to move the mulch and sift for worms at the same time. The end result is I end up with enough earth worms to start a new farm and I have discovered a new worm bed material that they like.

I consider these sort of losses of time very important to everyday business. I had the option to get out of the cold weather and just move the mulch as fast I could and be done with it. By taking the time to identify a new opportunity and examining my environment I have managed to create two outcomes when I set out to do one. The extra worm farm means I can now run twice the composting and I can now breed twice the amount of the large worms. Did I need to actually do this? No. I did not. But by doing so, I have now expanded my production capabilities by taking the extra time.

Had I decided this day to just look for worms in the mulch, I would have had to have sifted my way through all the mulch and dug out the worms. The mulch would not have gone very far. While I added an extra 1 hour to my 2 hour planned work I managed to do two things at once and reduce double handling. Spend 2 hours looking for worms? Spend 2 hours moving mulch? Save an hour by doing the extra hour.

Key points:

* Always investigate any opportunity that comes your way. You can not get anywhere with anything without taking time to look at opportunity. * Do not leave opportunity to be looked at later. By the time you decide to collect the worms, you've already moved all the mulch and lost your chance. * Almost always, to save time you must first take more time. This principle applies to many things. To save money you must make money. To make money you must spend money. To prevent breakdowns you must regularly maintain. Time saving outcomes must involve time spending first. The goal is to spend a little time, to save much time. * Opportunity that is found in the least likely places, is often the best kind to go after. I would never have guessed to check the top of a pile of mulch for these earth worms. And many small businesses that go for changes in unlikely places usually become big.
Always follow potential leads to profit, example from some gardening.
